title: The Trouble With Sitting Behind Our Desks
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a PD workshop question about whether teachers should sit at their desks during independent work time, Dave Stuart Jr. argues the practice is neither simply good nor bad but depends on what it signals to students. He grounds the discussion in the necessity of independent practice itself, noting that real learning requires students to do the individual work of writing, reading, or problem-solving rather than passively receiving instruction, and that getting a class to that point takes sustained classroom management and Woodenization. His central concern is Credibility: a teacher who habitually retreats to a desk, even while doing legitimate work like grading or feedback, risks signaling detachment from the class. Stuart's proposed fix is simple and low-cost — narrate what you're doing while students work independently, so the same desk-sitting reads as engaged partnership rather than checking out. He closes with the line that intentions don't build belief in a teacher's credibility; signals do.
points: Independent practice is a non-negotiable phase of learning because the person who does the work does the learning, so classrooms without any independent-work time risk students avoiding the work minds actually need to grow.

Whether desk-sitting harms a teacher's Credibility depends on the signal it sends, not the intention behind it — habitual retreat to the desk can read as detachment even when the teacher is doing beneficial work.
A simple verbal move — telling students specifically what you'll be doing while they work independently — converts desk time from a credibility risk into a visible display of being 'in it with them.'

Contrasting a narrated task ('While you read... I'll be going through the writing you did yesterday') against a bare task list ('Work on X until you finish it') shows how the same classroom setup can send opposite signals.

Getting students capable of productive independent practice is itself hard-won, requiring classroom management, stamina-building, and Woodenization before a teacher can even face this desk-sitting question.
quotes: The person who does the work does the learning; the mind changes through work as the body changes through work.

When we don't have independent work happening at all in our classrooms — choosing instead modes like direct instruction or collaborative learning — we run the risk of individual students avoiding the individual work it takes for a mind to learn.

If it becomes a habit, I run the risk of harming my Credibility with students. Even if I'm at work on something directly beneficial to them (e.g., feedback on their work), me habitually retreating to my desk while they work independently can send the signal that I'm detached from what they're doing.

While you read and respond to the article during the next 15 minutes, I'll periodically circulate to see if you have any questions. When I'm not circulating, I'll be going through the writing you did yesterday and making note of patterns we can address during revisions tomorrow.
The teacher may have the best of intentions — or heck, they may just be tired from this difficult, often-exhausting job we do! — but intentions don't build the Credibility belief. Signals do.
